# Resonant Activation in the Hopping Dynamics of Two-Mode Semiconductor Lasers

This study theoretically investigates the possibility of observing resonant activation in the hopping dynamics of two-mode semiconductor lasers. Resonant activation, a phenomenon in which the escape rate from a metastable state exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the characteristic time-scale of an external modulation, provides a compelling framework for understanding the switching behavior between competing lasing modes in these optical systems.

To explore this possibility, we conducted a series of simulations based on a rate-equations model. The dynamics were examined under two distinct driving conditions: random modulation and periodic modulation of the bias current. This dual approach allows us to assess the generality of the observed effects and to determine whether resonant activation emerges independently of the specific nature of the modulation.

In both modulation cases, the simulations reveal a consistent and characteristic behavior: the hopping times between the stable lasing modes reach a minimum at an optimal modulation time-scale. This non-monotonic dependence—where the switching dynamics are accelerated most efficiently at an intermediate modulation frequency—constitutes the hallmark signature of resonant activation.

To provide a deeper physical understanding of these results, we interpret the simulation data using an effective one-dimensional Langevin equation featuring multiplicative fluctuations. This reduced description captures the essential features of the mode-hopping dynamics and offers a transparent explanation of the mechanisms underlying the observed resonant activation phenomenon.

Importantly, the conclusions drawn from this analysis are not restricted to a single class of devices. They apply to both Edge Emitting Lasers and Vertical Cavity Surface Emitting Lasers, thereby enabling a range of experimental tests across these different optical systems. This broad applicability enhances the prospects for the direct experimental verification of resonant activation in semiconductor laser platforms.

# Resonant Activation in the Hopping Dynamics of Two-Mode Semiconductor Lasers

## Introduction

Semiconductor lasers operating in a two-mode regime constitute a rich platform for investigating noise-driven dynamical phenomena. In such systems, the laser output can spontaneously switch between two distinct lasing modes, a process that resembles the escape of a particle over a potential barrier separating two metastable states. When the barrier separating these modes fluctuates in time—either randomly or under an externally imposed periodic drive—the dynamics of mode-hopping can exhibit nontrivial dependencies on the characteristic time-scale of the modulation. Among these phenomena, resonant activation stands out as a counterintuitive effect in which the mean escape time between states is minimized for an optimal modulation time-scale.

## Theoretical Framework

In this study, we theoretically investigate the emergence of resonant activation in the hopping dynamics of two-mode semiconductor lasers. Our analysis is grounded in numerical simulations of the laser rate equations, which capture the coupled evolution of the optical field intensities and the carrier density within the active medium. To probe the influence of fluctuating barriers, we modulate the bias current of the laser using both random (stochastic) and periodic (deterministic) driving protocols. This modulation induces temporal variations in the effective potential landscape that governs the competition between the two lasing modes.

To gain physical insight into the underlying mechanism, we reduce the full multidimensional rate-equation description to an effective one-dimensional Langevin equation. In this reduced picture, a single collective variable—related to the relative intensity or population difference of the two modes—evolves in a bistable potential subject to noise. Crucially, the fluctuations entering this Langevin description are multiplicative rather than additive, reflecting the intensity-dependent nature of the noise sources intrinsic to semiconductor laser dynamics. This effective model allows us to connect the observed behavior to the broader theoretical literature on resonant activation in stochastic systems.

## Results

Our simulations reveal a clear signature of resonant activation: the mean hopping time between the two stable lasing modes exhibits a pronounced minimum as a function of the modulation time-scale of the bias current. When the modulation is very slow, the system experiences a quasi-static barrier and the escape dynamics are dominated by the highest instantaneous barrier configurations. Conversely, when the modulation is very fast, the system responds only to the time-averaged barrier. It is precisely in the intermediate regime—where the modulation time-scale matches the characteristic escape dynamics—that the hopping process is most efficient, yielding the shortest transition times.

This non-monotonic dependence is observed for both random and periodic modulation of the bias current, demonstrating the robustness of the resonant activation effect across different driving protocols. The consistency between the full rate-equation simulations and the reduced Langevin description confirms that the multiplicative-noise, one-dimensional model captures the essential physics of the phenomenon.

## Applicability and Experimental Prospects

Importantly, our findings are not restricted to a single class of devices. The resonant activation effect we describe applies to both Edge Emitting Lasers and Vertical Cavity Surface Emitting Lasers, two of the most widely employed semiconductor laser architectures. Because bias-current modulation is a readily accessible experimental control parameter, and because mode-hopping statistics can be directly monitored through intensity measurements, our results suggest a concrete route toward experimental verification of resonant activation in these optical systems.

## Conclusion

In summary, we have theoretically demonstrated that two-mode semiconductor lasers exhibit resonant activation when their bias current is modulated on an optimal time-scale, minimizing the hopping times between stable lasing modes. By bridging detailed rate-equation simulations with an effective one-dimensional Langevin framework featuring multiplicative fluctuations, this work provides both a quantitative and an intuitive understanding of the effect. The generality of the phenomenon across different laser types positions optical systems as promising and controllable testbeds for exploring resonant activation and related noise-assisted dynamical phenomena.

# The Legacy of Paul Langevin

The name Langevin holds a distinguished place in the history of physics. Paul Langevin, a French physicist born in 1872, made lasting contributions to our understanding of magnetism, statistical mechanics, and the behavior of particles in motion. Our appreciation of his work has only grown over the decades, as many of his ideas continue to shape modern science.

## The Langevin Equation

One of Langevin's most influential achievements is the equation that bears his name. The Langevin equation describes the motion of a particle suspended in a fluid, accounting for both the systematic forces acting upon it and the random, fluctuating forces caused by countless molecular collisions. Our study of Brownian motion owes much to this elegant mathematical framework, which bridges deterministic and probabilistic descriptions of nature.

The beauty of the Langevin approach lies in its simplicity and versatility. It has found applications far beyond its original context, extending into fields such as chemistry, biology, and even finance. Our modern simulations of molecular dynamics frequently rely on Langevin-based methods to model realistic thermal environments.

## Our Continued Debt to His Vision

Beyond his scientific discoveries, Langevin was a committed advocate for education and social progress. The values he championed—curiosity, rigor, and intellectual courage—remain relevant today. Our scientific community continues to build upon the foundations he helped establish.

In reflecting on his contributions, we recognize that the questions Langevin asked still guide our inquiries. The tools he developed remain essential, and our gratitude for his insight endures. His story reminds us that the pursuit of knowledge is a shared journey, one in which each generation adds to the work of those who came before.

# Resonant Activation in Two-Mode Semiconductor Laser Hopping Dynamics

## Abstract

We investigate the phenomenon of resonant activation in the mode-hopping dynamics of two-mode semiconductor lasers subject to a periodically modulated pump current. In the bistable regime, spontaneous emission noise drives stochastic transitions (hops) between two competing longitudinal modes, a process that can be described as thermally-activated escape over a fluctuating potential barrier. By modulating the pump at frequencies comparable to the characteristic barrier-fluctuation timescale, we demonstrate that the mean first-passage time for mode switching exhibits a pronounced minimum at an optimal modulation frequency—the hallmark of resonant activation. Using a two-mode rate-equation model incorporating cross-gain saturation and Langevin noise sources, we derive an effective one-dimensional Fokker-Planck description of the modal intensity dynamics and compute the switching rates as functions of modulation amplitude, frequency, and noise strength. Numerical simulations confirm that the hopping rate is maximized when the external driving synchronizes with the intrinsic relaxation of the modal competition, yielding a nonmonotonic dependence of the escape time on modulation frequency. We further show that the resonant activation peak is robust against variations in the gain-saturation coefficient but is sensitive to the degree of mode asymmetry. These results establish two-mode semiconductor lasers as a versatile optical platform for exploring noise-assisted barrier-crossing phenomena and suggest practical routes for controlling mode-selection stability and switching speed in optical bistable devices.

# Resonant Activation in Optical Systems: A Rate Equation and Langevin Dynamics Approach

## Abstract

Resonant activation—the phenomenon whereby the escape rate of a system over a fluctuating potential barrier exhibits a minimum as a function of the modulation timescale—has been extensively studied in chemical and biological contexts, yet its manifestation in optical systems remains comparatively unexplored. Here we present a theoretical and numerical investigation of resonant activation in semiconductor laser dynamics subject to fluctuating parameters and intrinsic noise. We formulate the problem in terms of coupled rate equations for the photon and carrier populations, augmented by stochastic Langevin terms that capture spontaneous emission noise and pump fluctuations. By modulating the effective potential barrier governing transitions between distinct dynamical states—such as the switch-on delay from below to above threshold—we demonstrate that the mean first-passage time attains a pronounced minimum at an optimal modulation frequency, the signature of resonant activation. Our analysis reveals that this optimum arises from the interplay between the characteristic relaxation oscillation timescale and the correlation time of the imposed noise. We apply the framework to two experimentally relevant device architectures: edge-emitting lasers, where the extended cavity geometry and longitudinal mode structure influence the noise-driven escape dynamics, and vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers (VCSELs), where the reduced active volume and polarization degrees of freedom enhance sensitivity to fluctuations. Numerical simulations of the Langevin equations corroborate the predictions of the rate-equation formalism and quantify how device-specific parameters—including cavity photon lifetime, carrier recombination rate, and spontaneous emission factor—modulate the resonant activation response. These results establish semiconductor lasers as a tunable and experimentally accessible platform for probing noise-assisted barrier crossing, with implications for optimizing switching performance, controlling turn-on jitter, and exploiting noise for enhanced dynamical response in photonic devices.

**Keywords:** resonant activation, semiconductor lasers, rate equations, Langevin dynamics, VCSELs, edge-emitting lasers, noise-induced transitions

# Abstract

We investigate the influence of modulation timescale on mode-hopping dynamics in two-mode lasers, focusing on how the frequency of an external periodic modulation governs the mean residence time in each lasing mode. Two-mode lasers exhibit bistability arising from gain competition between modes, with spontaneous emission noise driving stochastic transitions—mode hops—between the two stable operating states. By applying periodic modulation to the pump or mode coupling, we control the effective barrier separating the two modes and systematically vary the modulation period relative to the intrinsic relaxation and correlation timescales of the system.

We show that the mean mode-hopping time depends non-monotonically on the modulation frequency, exhibiting distinct regimes governed by the ratio of the modulation period to the internal system timescales. In the adiabatic (slow-modulation) limit, the system follows the instantaneous potential quasi-statically, and hopping times track the modulated barrier height. In the fast-modulation limit, the laser responds only to the time-averaged potential, and the modulation ceases to enhance switching. Between these limits, a resonant matching between the modulation timescale and the noise-activated escape timescale produces a pronounced modification of the hopping rate.

To explain these observations, we derive an effective one-dimensional Langevin equation for the modal intensity difference (or a suitably defined order parameter), in which the fast microscopic degrees of freedom are adiabatically eliminated to yield an effective double-well potential subject to noise and periodic driving. This reduced description captures the essential physics of the mode-hopping process and quantitatively reproduces the measured dependence of residence times on modulation timescale. Our results clarify the interplay between deterministic modulation and stochastic switching in bistable laser systems and provide a predictive framework for controlling mode selection through the temporal structure of external driving.
